verses.18:7: And the people of Israel were struck down there by the army of David, and a great slaughter took place on that day, of twenty thousand.
verses.18:8: Now the battle there was spread over the face of all the land, and there were many more of the people whom the forest had consumed than those whom the sword had devoured on that day.
verses.18:9: Now it happened that Absalom encountered the servants of David while riding on a mule; and when the mule had gone under a thick and great oak, his head caught fast in the oak, and while he was suspended between heaven and earth, the mule on which he had been riding passed on.
verses.18:10: Now someone saw this and reported it to Joab, saying, "I saw Absalom hanging from an oak."
verses.18:11: And Joab said to the man who had reported it to him, "If you saw him, why did you not pierce him to the ground, and I would have given you ten shekels of silver and one belt?"
verses.18:12: And he said to Joab, "If you were to weigh out a thousand pieces of silver in my hands, I would by no means lay my hand on the king's son; for in our hearing the king commanded you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, 'Guard the boy Absalom for me.'
verses.18:13: But even if I had acted boldly against my own life, this could by no means have been hidden from the king, and you would stand on the opposite side?"
verses.18:14: And Joab said, "Not as you wish, but I will attack him before you." So he took three lances in his hand and drove them into the heart of Absalom; and while he was still quivering, caught in the oak,
verses.18:15: ten young men, armor-bearers of Joab, ran up and, striking him, killed him.
verses.18:16: Then Joab sounded the trumpet and held back the people, so that they would not pursue fleeing Israel, wanting to spare the multitude.
verses.18:17: And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest, and they piled up a very great heap of stones over him; meanwhile, all Israel fled to their tents.
verses.18:18: Now Absalom, while he was still living, had erected for himself the pillar which is in the Valley of the King; for he had said, "I have no son, and this will be a memorial of my name." And he called the pillar by his own name, and it is called the Hand of Absalom to this day.
verses.18:19: Now Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "I will run and report to the king that the Lord has rendered judgment for him from the hand of his enemies."
verses.18:20: To him Joab said, "You will not be a messenger on this day, but you will bring news on another; today I do not want you to bring news, for the king's son is dead."
verses.18:21: And Joab said to Cushi, "Go and report to the king what you have seen." Cushi bowed down to Joab and ran.
verses.18:22: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "What prevents it if I also run after Cushi?" And Joab said to him, "Why do you want to run, my son? You will not be a bearer of good news."
verses.18:23: And he answered, "What then if I run?" And he said to him, "Run." So Ahimaaz, running by the shorter way, passed Cushi.
verses.18:24: Now David was sitting between the two gates; and the watchman, who was on the top of the gate above the wall, lifting up his eyes, saw a man running alone.
verses.18:25: And crying out, he informed the king; and the king said, "If he is alone, there is good news in his mouth." Now as he was hurrying and coming nearer,
verses.18:26: the watchman saw another man running, and shouting on the roof, he said, "Another man appears to me, running alone." And the king said, "This one also is a good messenger."
verses.18:27: Now the watchman said, "I observe the running of the first to be like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man, and he comes carrying good news."
verses.18:28: Then Ahimaaz, calling out, said to the king, "Hail, king." And bowing down to the king before him, prostrate to the ground, he said, "Blessed be the Lord your God, who has hemmed in the men who lifted up their hands against my lord the king."
verses.18:29: And the king said, "Is there peace for the boy Absalom?" And Ahimaaz said, "I saw a great uproar when your servant Joab, king, sent me, your servant; I know nothing else."
verses.18:30: To him the king said, "Step aside and stand here." And when he had stepped aside and was standing,
verses.18:31: Cushi appeared, and as he came, he said, "I bring good news, my lord the king; for the Lord has judged in your favor today from the hand of all who rose up against you."
verses.18:32: And the king said to Cushi, "Is there peace for the boy Absalom?" Answering him, Cushi said, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against him for evil, become like the boy."
verses.19:1: So the king, grieved, went up to the upper room of the gate and wept. And as he walked, he kept saying this: "My son Absalom, Absalom my son! Who would grant me that I might die in your place, Absalom my son, my son Absalom?"
verses.19:2: Now it was reported to Joab that the king was weeping and mourning for his son.
verses.19:3: And the victory was turned into mourning on that day for all the people, for the people heard it said on that day, "The king is grieving over his son."
verses.19:4: And on that day the people shrank from entering the city, just as a people routed and fleeing from battle is accustomed to shrink away.
verses.19:5: Meanwhile, the king covered his head and kept crying out with a loud voice, "My son Absalom, Absalom my son, my son!"
verses.19:6: Then Joab went into the house to the king and said, "Today you have put to shame the faces of all your servants, who saved your life, and the lives of your sons and your daughters, and the lives of your wives, and the lives of your concubines.
verses.19:7: You love those who hate you, and you hate those who love you. And today you have shown that you do not care about your commanders and your servants; and now I truly know that if Absalom were alive and all of us had died, then it would please you.
verses.19:8: Now therefore, rise, go out, and speak to your servants to satisfy them; for I swear to you by the Lord that if you do not go out, not even one will remain with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evils that have come upon you from your youth until the present."
verses.19:9: So the king rose and sat in the gate, and it was reported to all the people that the king was sitting in the gate. And the entire multitude came before the king; but Israel fled to their tents.
verses.19:10: All the people also were disputing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies; he himself saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled from the land because of Absalom.
verses.19:11: But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. How long will you keep silent and not bring the king back?"
verses.19:12: Now King David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, saying, "Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, 'Why are you coming last to bring the king back to his house?'" (Now the word of all Israel had reached the king in his house.)
verses.19:13: "'You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring the king back?'
verses.19:14: And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? May God do this to me, and add this as well, if you are not commander of the army before me at all times in place of Joab.'"
verses.19:15: And he inclined the heart of all the men of Judah as of one man, and they sent to the king, saying, "Return, you and all your servants."
verses.19:16: So the king returned and came as far as the Jordan; and all Judah came as far as Gilgal to meet the king and to bring him across the Jordan.
verses.19:17: Now Shimei the son of Gera, the son of Jemini, from Bahurim, hurried and went down with the men of Judah to meet King David,
verses.19:18: with a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba, the attendant of the house of Saul; and his fifteen sons and twenty servants were with him. And rushing into the Jordan, before the king
verses.19:19: they crossed the fords to bring the king's household across and to do according to his command. Now Shimei the son of Gera, having fallen prostrate before the king when he had already crossed the Jordan,
verses.19:20: said to him, "Do not count iniquity against me, my lord, and do not remember the wrongs of your servant on the day you went out from Jerusalem, my lord the king, and do not take it to heart, king.
verses.19:21: For I, your servant, acknowledge my sin; and for this reason I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph, and I have come down to meet my lord the king."
verses.19:22: Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, "Should Shimei not be put to death for these words, because he cursed the Lord's anointed?"
verses.19:23: And David said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why are you becoming an adversary to me today? Should a man then be put to death in Israel today? Or do I not know that today I have been made king over Israel?"
verses.19:24: And the king said to Shimei, "You will not die." And he swore to him.
verses.19:25: Mephibosheth the son of Saul also came down to meet the king, with unwashed feet and an untrimmed beard; and he had not washed his clothes from the day the king had gone out until the day of his return in peace.
verses.19:26: And when he met the king in Jerusalem, the king said to him, "Why did you not come with me, Mephibosheth?"
verses.19:27: And he answered and said, "My lord the king, my servant despised me; and I, your servant, told him to saddle a donkey for me so that I might mount it and go with the king, for I, your servant, am lame.
verses.19:28: Moreover, he has also accused me, your servant, to you, my lord the king. But you, my lord the king, are like an angel of God; do what is pleasing to you.
verses.19:29: For my father's house was nothing except liable to death before my lord the king, yet you placed me, your servant, among the guests at your table. What just complaint, then, do I have, or what more can I cry out to the king?"
verses.19:30: Then the king said to him, "Why do you speak any more? What I have spoken is settled: you and Ziba, divide the possessions."
verses.19:31: And Mephibosheth answered the king, "Let him even take it all, since my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house."
verses.19:32: Barzillai the Gileadite also, coming down from Rogelim, brought the king across the Jordan, ready even to escort him beyond the river.
verses.19:33: Now Barzillai the Gileadite was very old, that is, eighty years old; and he himself had provided food for the king while he was staying in the camp, for he was an exceedingly wealthy man.
verses.19:34: So the king said to Barzillai, "Come with me, so that you may rest securely with me in Jerusalem."
verses.19:35: And Barzillai said to the king, "How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
verses.19:36: I am eighty years old today. Are my senses strong enough to discern sweet or bitter? Or can food and drink delight your servant? Or can I any longer hear the voice of male and female singers? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
verses.19:37: I, your servant, will go a little way from the Jordan with you; I do not need this repayment,
verses.19:38: but I beg that I, your servant, may return and die in my city, and be buried beside the tomb of my father and my mother. But there is your servant Chimham; let him go with you, my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."
verses.19:39: So the king said to him, "Let Chimham cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever pleases you; and everything you ask of me, you will obtain."
verses.19:40: And when all the people and the king had crossed the Jordan, the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him; and he returned to his place.
verses.19:41: Then the king passed on to Gilgal, and Chimham with him. Now all the people of Judah had brought the king across, and only half of the people of Israel had been present.
verses.19:42: Therefore all the men of Israel, coming together to the king, said to him, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, and all the men of David with him?"
verses.19:43: And every man of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is closer to me. Why are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten anything from the king, or have gifts been given to us?"
verses.19:44: And the man of Israel answered the men of Judah and said, "I am greater by ten parts with the king, and David belongs more to me than to you. Why have you done me wrong, and why was it not reported to me first, so that I might bring back my king?" But the men of Judah answered the men of Israel more harshly.
verses.20:1: It also happened that there was a man of Belial there, named Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Jeminite; and he blew the horn and said, "We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse; return to your tents, Israel!"
verses.20:2: So all Israel separated from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri; but the men of Judah clung to their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem.
verses.20:3: And when the king came to his house in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubine women whom he had left behind to guard the house and placed them under guard, providing food for them; and he did not go in to them, but they were shut up until the day of their death, living in widowhood.
verses.20:4: Then the king said to Amasa, "Summon all the men of Judah to me by the third day, and be present yourself."
verses.20:5: So Amasa went out to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the appointed time that the king had set for him.
verses.20:6: Then David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri is going to afflict us more than Absalom; therefore, take your lord's servants and pursue him, or else he might find fortified cities and escape us."
verses.20:7: So Joab's men went out with him, along with the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and all the mighty men went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.20:8: And when they were beside the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came and met them. Now Joab was dressed in a tunic fitted tightly to the measure of his frame, and over it he was belted with a sword hanging down to his hips in a sheath, which was so fashioned that at a slight movement it could come out and strike.
verses.20:9: So Joab said to Amasa, "Greetings, my brother." And with his right hand he took hold of Amasa's chin, as if to kiss him.
verses.20:10: Now Amasa did not notice the sword that Joab had; and he struck him in the side and poured out his intestines onto the ground, and did not add a second wound; and he died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.20:11: Meanwhile, certain men from Joab's companions, standing beside Amasa's corpse, said, "Look at the one who wanted to be David's companion in place of Joab!"
verses.20:12: Now Amasa lay spattered with blood in the middle of the road. A certain man saw this, that all the people were stopping to look at him, and he removed Amasa from the road into a field and covered him with a garment, so that those passing by would not stop because of him.
verses.20:13: So once he had been removed from the road, every man passed on, following Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.20:14: Meanwhile, he had passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and all the chosen men had gathered to him.
verses.20:15: So they came and attacked him in Abel and in Beth-maacah, and they surrounded the city with siegeworks, and the city was besieged; and all the crowd that was with Joab was working to destroy the walls.
verses.20:16: Then a wise woman cried out from the city, "Listen, listen! Tell Joab, 'Come near here, and I will speak with you.'"
verses.20:17: And when he had approached her, she said to him, "Are you Joab?" And he answered, "I am." And she spoke to him in this way: "Listen to the words of your maidservant." And he answered, "I am listening."
verses.20:18: And again she said, "A saying used to be spoken in an old proverb: 'Let those who inquire, inquire in Abel,' and so they brought matters to completion.
verses.20:19: Am I not the one who answers truth in Israel, and you seek to overthrow a city and destroy a mother in Israel? Why do you bring the inheritance of the Lord to ruin?"
verses.20:20: And Joab answered and said, "Far be it, far be this from me! I am not bringing ruin, nor am I demolishing.
verses.20:21: That is not how the matter stands, but a man from Mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by surname, has lifted up his hand against King David. Hand him over alone, and we will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall."
verses.20:22: So she went in to all the people and spoke to them wisely; and they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. And he blew the trumpet, and they withdrew from the city, each one to his tents; and Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verses.20:23: Now Joab was over all the army of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
verses.20:24: Adoram was over the tribute, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder.
verses.20:25: Sheva was scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
verses.20:26: And Ira the Jairite was David's priest.
verses.21:1: A famine also occurred in the days of David for three years continuously, and David consulted the oracle of the Lord. And the Lord said, "Because of Saul and his house of bloodshed, because he killed the Gibeonites."
verses.21:2: Therefore, having called the Gibeonites, the king spoke to them (now the Gibeonites were not of the sons of Israel, but the remnant of the Amorites; for the sons of Israel had sworn to them, and Saul wanted to strike them down in zeal, as if for the sons of Israel and Judah).
verses.21:3: David therefore said to the Gibeonites, "What should I do for you? And what will be the atonement for you, so that you may bless the inheritance of the Lord?"
verses.21:4: And the Gibeonites said to him, "We have no dispute over silver and gold, but against Saul and against his house; nor do we want any man of Israel to be killed." To them the king said, "What then do you want me to do for you?"
verses.21:5: They said to the king, "The man who crushed us and oppressed us unjustly, we must wipe out in such a way that not even one remains from his lineage in all the borders of Israel.
verses.21:6: Let seven men of his sons be given to us, so that we may crucify them to the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, once the chosen of the Lord." And the king said, "I will give them."
verses.21:7: And the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the oath of the Lord that had been between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.
verses.21:8: So the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel the son of Barzillai, who was a Meholathite,
verses.21:9: and he gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites, who crucified them on the mountain before the Lord; and these seven fell killed together in the first days of the harvest, as the reaping of the barley was beginning.
verses.21:10: Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, taking sackcloth, spread it out for herself on the rock from the beginning of the harvest until water dripped upon them from the sky; and she did not allow the birds to tear them by day, nor the beasts by night.
verses.21:11: And it was reported to David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.
verses.21:12: And David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, in which the Philistines had hanged them when they had killed Saul on Gilboa;
verses.21:13: and he carried away from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son; and gathering the bones of those who had been affixed,
verses.21:14: they buried them with the bones of Saul and of Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin, on the side, in the tomb of Kish his father; and they did everything that the king had commanded, and God became favorable again to the land after these things.
verses.21:15: Now a battle of the Philistines occurred again against Israel, and David went down, and his servants with him, and they were fighting against the Philistines. And as David grew faint,
verses.21:16: Ishbi-benob, who was of the race of Arapha, the iron of whose spear weighed three hundred ounces, and who was girded with a new sword, attempted to strike down David.
verses.21:17: And Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his defense, and struck the Philistine and killed him. Then the men of David swore, saying, "You will no longer go out with us to war, so that you do not extinguish the lamp of Israel."
verses.21:18: There was also a second war in Gob against the Philistines; then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, of the lineage of Arapha, of the race of the giants.
verses.21:19: There was also a third war in Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus the son of Saltus, an embroiderer, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weavers' beam.
verses.21:20: There was a fourth war in Gath, in which there was a tall man who had six digits on each hand and foot, that is, twenty-four; and he was of the stock of Arapha.
verses.21:21: And he reviled Israel; but Jonathan the son of Shimea, the brother of David, struck him down.
verses.21:22: These four were born of Arapha in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and of his servants.
verses.22:1: Now David spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
verses.22:2: And he said, "The Lord is my rock, and my might, and my savior.
verses.22:3: My strong God, I will hope in Him; my shield and the horn of my salvation, the One who lifts me up and my refuge, my savior: You will deliver me from iniquity.
verses.22:4: I will call upon the Lord, who is praiseworthy, and I will be saved from my enemies.
verses.22:5: For the crushings of death surrounded me; the torrents of Belial terrified me.
verses.22:6: The cords of the underworld surrounded me; the snares of death confronted me.
verses.22:7: In my tribulation I will call upon the Lord, and to my God I will cry out; and from His temple He will hear my voice, and my cry will come to His ears.
verses.22:8: The earth heaved and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were shaken and convulsed, because He was angry with them.
verses.22:9: Smoke rose from His nostrils, and fire from His mouth will devour; coals were kindled by Him.
verses.22:10: He bent the heavens and descended, and thick darkness was beneath His feet.
verses.22:11: And He ascended upon the cherubim and flew, and glided upon the wings of the wind.
verses.22:12: He set darkness around Himself as a hiding place, sifting waters from the clouds of the heavens.
verses.22:13: From the brilliance in His presence, coals of fire were kindled.
verses.22:14: The Lord will thunder from heaven, and the Most High will give forth His voice.
verses.22:15: He sent arrows and dispersed them; lightning, and He consumed them.
verses.22:16: And the outpourings of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were uncovered at the rebuke of the Lord, at the blast of the breath of His fury.
verses.22:17: He sent from on high and took me up, and drew me out from many waters.
verses.22:18: He delivered me from my most powerful enemy, and from those who hated me, because they were stronger than I.
verses.22:19: He confronted me on the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my support.
verses.22:20: And He brought me out into a broad place; He delivered me, because I was pleasing to Him.
verses.22:21: The Lord will reward me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands He will repay me.
verses.22:22: For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and I have not acted impiously away from my God.
verses.22:23: For all His judgments are before me, and I have not put His precepts away from me.
verses.22:24: And I will be perfect with Him, and I will guard myself from my iniquity.
verses.22:25: And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands in the sight of His eyes.
verses.22:26: With the holy one You will be holy, and with the strong one You will be perfect.
verses.22:27: With the chosen one You will be chosen, and with the perverse one You will be perverted.
verses.22:28: And You will save the poor people, and with Your eyes You will humble the lofty.
verses.22:29: For You are my lamp, Lord, and You, Lord, will illuminate my darkness.
verses.22:30: For in You I will run girded; in my God I will spring over a wall.
verses.22:31: God: His way is spotless; the utterance of the Lord is tested by fire; He is a shield to all who hope in Him.
verses.22:32: Who is God besides the Lord, and who is strong besides our God?
verses.22:33: God is the One who girded me with strength and leveled my perfect way,
verses.22:34: making my feet equal to those of stags and setting me upon my high places;
verses.22:35: teaching my hands for battle and fashioning my arms like a bronze bow.
verses.22:36: You gave me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness multiplied me.
verses.22:37: You will widen my steps beneath me, and my ankles will not falter.
verses.22:38: I will pursue my enemies and crush them, and I will not turn back until I consume them.
verses.22:39: I will consume them and shatter them, so that they will not rise up; they will fall beneath my feet.
verses.22:40: You girded me with strength for battle; You bowed down beneath me those who resist me.
verses.22:41: You made my enemies turn their backs to me, those who hate me, and I will destroy them.
verses.22:42: They will cry out, and there will be no one to save; to the Lord, and He will not hear them.
verses.22:43: I will wipe them out like the dust of the earth; like the mud of the streets I will pulverize them and shatter them.
verses.22:44: You will save me from the disputes of my people; You will preserve me as head of the nations; a people whom I do not know will serve me.
verses.22:45: The sons of foreigners will resist me; upon the hearing of the ear they will obey me.
verses.22:46: The sons of foreigners have faded away, and they will be constricted in their narrow confines.
verses.22:47: The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and the strong God of my salvation will be exalted.
verses.22:48: God, You who give acts of vengeance to me and cast down peoples beneath me,
verses.22:49: You who bring me out from my enemies and lift me up from those who resist me, You will deliver me from the unjust man.
verses.22:50: Therefore I will give praise to You, Lord, among the nations, and I will sing to Your name.
verses.22:51: He magnifies the deliverances of His king and shows mercy to His anointed, David, and to his seed forever."
verses.23:1: Now these are the final words of David. David the son of Jesse said; the man to whom it was appointed concerning the anointed of the God of Jacob, the eminent psalmist of Israel, said:
verses.23:2: "The Spirit of the Lord has spoken through me, and His word through my tongue.
verses.23:3: The God of Israel said to me, the Strong One of Israel spoke: 'A ruler of men, a just ruler in the fear of God,
verses.23:4: is like the light of dawn glowing when the sun rises in a morning without clouds, and like grass sprouting from the earth by rains.'
verses.23:5: Nor is my house so great before God that He should enter into an eternal covenant with me, firm in all things and secured. For it is all my salvation and every desire, nor is there anything from it that does not sprout.
verses.23:6: But transgressors will all be torn out like thorns, which are not picked up with hands.
verses.23:7: And if anyone wishes to touch them, he will be armed with iron and a lance shaft; and kindled with fire, they will be burned up to nothing."
verses.23:8: These are the names of the mighty men of David: the one sitting in the chair, the wisest chief among the three; he is like the most tender little worm of wood, who killed eight hundred in a single assault.
verses.23:9: After him was Eleazar the son of his uncle, an Ahohite, among the three mighty men who were with David when they taunted the Philistines, and they were gathered there for battle.
verses.23:10: And when the men of Israel had gone up, he himself stood and struck down the Philistines until his hand gave out and grew stiff with the sword; and the Lord worked a great deliverance on that day; and the people who had fled returned to strip the spoils of those who were killed.
verses.23:11: And after him was Shammah the son of Agee from Harar. And the Philistines were gathered at a garrison, for there was a field there full of lentils. And when the people had fled from before the Philistines,
verses.23:12: he stood in the middle of the field and defended it, and struck down the Philistines; and the Lord worked a great deliverance.
verses.23:13: Moreover, three who were chiefs among the thirty had also gone down earlier and had come at harvest time to David in the cave of Adullam; and the camp of the Philistines was pitched in the Valley of Giants.
verses.23:14: And David was in the stronghold, while the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem.
verses.23:15: Therefore David had a longing and said, "Oh, if only someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern that is in Bethlehem beside the gate!"
verses.23:16: So the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, and drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem that was beside the gate, and brought it to David; but he would not drink, and instead poured it out as a libation to the Lord,
verses.23:17: saying, "May the Lord be merciful to me, that I not do this! Shall I drink the blood of these men who went out, and the peril of their lives?" Therefore he would not drink. The three strongest men did these things.
verses.23:18: Abishai also, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three. He is the one who raised his spear against three hundred, whom he killed; he was renowned among the three,
verses.23:19: and more honored among the three, and he was their chief, yet he had not attained to the first three.
verses.23:20: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, a most valiant man of great deeds, from Kabzeel: he himself struck down two lions of Moab, and he went down and struck down a lion in the middle of a cistern in the days of snow.
verses.23:21: He also killed an Egyptian man, a man who was a spectacle to see, having a spear in his hand; and so, when he had gone down to him with a staff, he wrenched the spear by force from the hand of the Egyptian and killed him with his own spear.
verses.23:22: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did these things.
verses.23:23: And he too was renowned among the three strong men who were more honored among the thirty; nevertheless, he had not attained to the three. And David made him his confidential counselor, in charge of secret affairs.
verses.23:24: Asahel the brother of Joab was among the thirty; Elhanan the son of his uncle, from Bethlehem,
verses.23:25: Shammah from Harod, Elika from Harod,
verses.23:26: Helez from Palti, Ira the son of Ikkesh from Tekoa,
verses.23:27: Abiezer from Anathoth, Mebunnai from Hushah,
verses.23:28: Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,
verses.23:29: Heled the son of Baanah, also a Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai from Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin,
verses.23:30: Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai from the brook of Gaash,
verses.23:31: Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth from Barhum,
verses.23:32: Eliahba from Shaalbon; the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,
verses.23:33: Shammah from Harar, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,
verses.23:34: Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
verses.23:35: Hezrai from Carmel, Paarai from Arab,
verses.23:36: Igal the son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani from Gad,
verses.23:37: Zelek from Ammon, Naharai the Beerothite, armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,
verses.23:38: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb also an Ithrite,
verses.23:39: Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
verses.24:1: And the fury of the Lord raged again against Israel, and stirred up David against them to say, "Go, number Israel and Judah."
verses.24:2: And the king said to Joab, the commander of his army, "Go through all the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, so that I may know their number."
verses.24:3: And Joab said to the king, "May the Lord your God add to your people, as many as they are now, and multiply them a hundredfold again in the sight of my lord the king; but what does my lord the king want for himself in a matter of this kind?"
verses.24:4: However, the word of the king prevailed over the words of Joab and of the commanders of the army; and Joab and the commander of the soldiers went out from the presence of the king to number the people of Israel.
verses.24:5: And when they had crossed over the Jordan, they came to Aroer, to the right of the city that is in the valley of Gad,
verses.24:6: and through Jazer they passed into Gilead and into the lower land of Hodshi, and they came to the woodlands of Dan. And going around near Sidon,
verses.24:7: they passed near the walls of Tyre and all the land of the Hivite and the Canaanite, and they came to the south of Judah, to Beersheba;
verses.24:8: and when the entire land had been surveyed, they arrived in Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days.
verses.24:9: Therefore Joab gave the number of the enrollment of the people to the king; and there were found of Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and of Judah five hundred thousand fighting men.
verses.24:10: But the heart of David struck him after the people were numbered; and David said to the Lord, "I have sinned greatly in this deed; but I pray, Lord, that You take away the iniquity of Your servant, because I have acted very foolishly."
verses.24:11: And so David rose in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet and seer of David, saying,
verses.24:12: "Go, and speak to David: 'This is what the Lord says: The choice of three things is given to you; choose one of these that you wish, so that I may do it to you.'"
verses.24:13: And when Gad had come to David, he reported to him, saying, "Either famine will come upon you in your land for seven years, or for three months you will flee from your adversaries and they will pursue you, or else for three days there will be pestilence in your land. Now therefore consider, and see what word I should answer to Him who sent me."
verses.24:14: And David said to Gad, "I am in great distress; yet it is better that I fall into the hands of the Lord (for His mercies are many) than into the hands of men."
verses.24:15: And the Lord sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning until the appointed time; and seventy thousand men of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba.
verses.24:16: And when the angel of the Lord had stretched out his hand over Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord had compassion over the affliction and said to the angel who was striking the people, "It is enough; now hold back your hand." Now the angel of the Lord was beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
verses.24:17: And David said to the Lord when he had seen the angel striking down the people, "It is I who have sinned; I have acted wickedly; these who are sheep, what have they done? Let Your hand, I plead, be turned against me and against the house of my father."
verses.24:18: And Gad came to David on that day and said to him, "Go up and set up an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
verses.24:19: And David went up according to the word of Gad, which the Lord had commanded him.
verses.24:20: And Araunah looked out and noticed the king and his servants coming across to him;
verses.24:21: and going out, he paid homage to the king with his face bowed to the ground, and said, "What is the reason that my lord the king has come to his servant?" David said to him, "To buy the threshing floor from you and build an altar to the Lord, so that the slaughter that is raging among the people may cease."
verses.24:22: And Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up as it pleases him; you have oxen for a burnt offering, and the cart, and the yokes of the oxen for use as firewood."
verses.24:23: Araunah the king gave all things to the king; and Araunah said to the king, "May the Lord your God accept your vow."
verses.24:24: Answering him, the king said, "By no means as you wish, but I will buy it from you for a price, and I will not offer to the Lord my God burnt offerings that cost nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
verses.24:25: And David built an altar there to the Lord and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings; and the Lord became merciful to the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.

notes.1:18: The Vulgate renders Hebrew Sefer ha-Yashar ("Book of Jashar") as libro justorum ("book of the righteous") and includes the additional opening line "Take thought, Israel, for those who have died, wounded on your high places," reflecting the Septuagint tradition alongside the Hebrew-based line in 1:19.
notes.1:21: Latin abjectus est ("was cast aside") differs from the Masoretic Text ("was defiled"), and masculine unctus ("anointed") leaves open whether it refers to Saul or to his oiled shield.
notes.1:26: The final sentence, "Just as a mother loves her only son, so I loved you," is a distinctly Vulgate (and Old Latin) reading not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.2:8: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Mahanaim ("Two Camps") as the common noun castra ("the camp"; likewise in 2:12 and 2:29) and reads circumduxit ("led him around") rather than "brought him over."
notes.2:9: Latin Gessuri ("Geshuri," i.e., Geshurites) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "the Ashurites."
notes.2:16: Latin Ager robustorum ("Field of the Strong") translates the Hebrew place name Helkath-hazzurim (meaning "Field of Sword-Edges" or "Field of Flints").
notes.2:24: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew place names Ammah and Giah as common nouns: collem aquæductus ("hill of the aqueduct") and vallis ("valley").
notes.2:26: Latin an ignoras quod periculosa sit desperatio? ("Or do you not know that desperation is dangerous?") is a distinctly Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end?"
notes.2:27: The Clementine Vulgate reads si locutus fuisses ("if you had spoken") without the negative found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("if you had not spoken"), and uses Dominus ("the Lord") where the Hebrew has "God."
notes.2:29: The Vulgate gives the proper name Beth-horon where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Bithron (a district or ravine east of the Jordan).
notes.3:8: The Vulgate reads adversum Judam ("against Judah"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "that belongs to Judah."
notes.3:21: The Vulgate has the first-person singular verb ineam ("that I may enter into a covenant with you"), whereas the Hebrew has the third-person plural ("that they may make a covenant with you").
notes.3:22: The Vulgate reads caesis latronibus ("having struck down the raiders"), whereas the Hebrew reads simply "from a raid."
notes.3:29: Vulgate tenens fusum ("one who holds a spindle") translates a debated Hebrew phrase that may mean "leaning on a crutch" or "staff," suggesting someone unfit for warfare and reduced to spinning.
notes.3:33: The Vulgate renders David's lament as a forceful statement (Nequaquam ... mortuus est, "By no means did Abner die") using ignavi ("cowards"), whereas the Hebrew poses a rhetorical question ("Should Abner die as a fool dies?").
notes.4:3: The Vulgate reads usque ad tempus illud ("until that time"), whereas the Hebrew reads "to this day."
notes.4:5: The Vulgate includes the sleeping female doorkeeper cleaning wheat (shared with the Septuagint) at the end of verse 5 alongside the assassins' secret entry taking ears of wheat in verse 6 (reflecting the Hebrew), preserving both textual traditions.
notes.4:10: The Vulgate reads cui oportebat mercedem dare pro nuntio ("to whom it was fitting to give a reward for the message"), an ironic rendering of a difficult Hebrew clause ("which was the reward I gave him for his news").
notes.5:8: The Vulgate explicitly supplies "had offered a reward" (proposuerat ... praemium) where the Hebrew sentence is elliptical, renders the difficult Hebrew term tsinnor ("water shaft") as "the pipes of the rooftops" (domatum fistulas), and reads "into the temple" (in templum) where the Hebrew reads "into the house."
notes.5:12: The Vulgate reads "over His people Israel" (super populum suum Israel), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for the sake of His people Israel."
notes.5:20: The Vulgate translates the verb explaining Baal-perazim as "has divided ... are divided" (divisit ... dividuntur), rather than the Hebrew "has broken through."
notes.5:23: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Vulgate includes David's direct question to the Lord ("Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will You deliver them into my hands?"), and renders the Hebrew trees (bekha'im, often "balsam" or "mulberry trees") as "pear trees" (pyrorum, also in 5:24).
notes.6:2: The Vulgate renders Hebrew Baale-judah as a descriptive phrase, "of the men of Judah" (de viris Juda), rather than a place name.
notes.6:3: The Vulgate treats in Gabaa ("in Gibeah") as a proper name modifying Abinadab ("who was in Gibeah," also in 6:4), where the Hebrew may be read "on the hill"; in 6:4 the Vulgate also specifies that Ahio was "guarding the ark of God" (custodiens arcam Dei).
notes.6:8: The Vulgate reads "was grieved" (contristatus est) where the Hebrew reads "was angry," and translates the place name Perez-uzzah literally into Latin as Percussio Ozae ("Striking of Uzzah").
notes.6:12: The final clause ("and there were with David seven choirs, and a sacrificial calf") is a Vulgate reading shared with the Septuagint tradition and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; similarly in 6:13 the Vulgate reads "a ram" (arietem) rather than "a fatling," and in 6:15 "the ark of the covenant of the Lord" (arcam testamenti Domini).
notes.6:19: The Vulgate renders two rare Hebrew food terms as "one piece of roasted beef" (assaturam bubulae carnis unam) and "fine flour fried in oil" (similam frixam oleo); the Hebrew terms are usually understood as a portion of meat (or a date cake) and a raisin cake.
notes.7:2: Vulgate "in medio pellium" ("in the midst of skins") specifies animal skins rather than the Masoretic Text's "curtains."
notes.7:10: Vulgate "sub eo" ("beneath it") literally renders the Hebrew idiom meaning "in its own place."
notes.7:19: Vulgate "lex Adam" ("the law of Adam") retains Hebrew "ha-adam" ("mankind" or "humanity") as the proper name Adam.
notes.7:23: Vulgate "gentem, et deum ejus" ("a nation and its god") uses singular nouns in an elliptical clause without an explicit verb such as "driving out."
notes.7:26: Vulgate "coram Domino" ("before the Lord") reads in the third person where the Masoretic Text reads "before You"; similarly in 7:29 Vulgate "Incipe" ("Begin") renders the Hebrew verb meaning "be pleased."
notes.8:1: Vulgate "frenum tributi" ("the bridle of tribute") interprets the obscure Hebrew phrase "Metheg-ammah," which is often taken as a place name.
notes.8:2: Vulgate "duos funiculos, unum ad occidendum, et unum ad vivificandum" counts two cords in total (one for death and one for life), whereas the Masoretic Text specifies two cords to put to death and one full cord to keep alive.
notes.8:3: Vulgate "Adarezer" (Hadarezer) here, like "Thou" (Tou) in 8:9-10, preserves the name forms matching 1 Chronicles 18 rather than Masoretic 2 Samuel's "Hadadezer" and "Toi."
notes.8:13: Vulgate "capta Syria in valle Salinarum" reads "Syria" (with the Masoretic Text's "Aram" against the Septuagint's "Edom") and renders the valley literally as "Salt Pits"; in 8:14 the Vulgate uses the Greco-Latin name "Idumea" for Edom.
notes.9:11: Vulgate "comedet super mensam meam" ("will eat at my table") uses the future tense and retains the Masoretic Text's first-person "my table" without a change of speaker, whereas the Septuagint reads "David's table" as narrator commentary.
notes.9:12: Vulgate "cognatio" ("family" or "kindred") renders the Hebrew phrase meaning "all who dwelt in the house."
notes.10:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom "made themselves odious" as "done an injury" (injuriam fecissent), and treats Istob (Ishtob) as a proper name where the Hebrew is usually read as "the men of Tob."
notes.10:12: The Vulgate reads singular "city" (civitate), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has plural "cities."
notes.10:16: The Vulgate preserves the form Adarezer ("Hadarezer," matching 1 Chronicles and the Septuagint) rather than the Masoretic "Hadadezer," and reads "brought their army" (adduxit eorum exercitum) where the Masoretic Text has "they came to Helam."
notes.10:19: The clause "they were terrified, and fifty-eight thousand fled before Israel" is a distinctly Vulgate reading (stemming from the Old Latin tradition) absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; likewise "in support of" (in præsidio) corresponds to Hebrew "servants/vassals."
notes.11:2: The Vulgate distinctly locates this scene "after midday" (post meridiem, rather than Hebrew "at evening") and places Bathsheba "on her roof" (super solarium suum), whereas the Hebrew says David saw her "from the roof."
notes.11:4: Latin statimque sanctificata est ("and immediately she was purified/sanctified") places Bathsheba's ritual purification immediately after the encounter, whereas the Hebrew clause is commonly read as a parenthetical explanation of her preceding bath.
notes.11:11: The Vulgate explicitly reads "the ark of God" (Arca Dei, where the Hebrew has simply "the ark") and "on the face of the earth" (super faciem terræ, where the Hebrew has "in the open field").
notes.11:21: The Vulgate preserves Gideon's original name Jerobaal ("Jerubbaal," matching Judges and the Septuagint) rather than the Masoretic dysphemism "Jerubbesheth."
notes.11:25: The Vulgate addresses Joab with "Strengthen your warriors ... and encourage them" (bellatores tuos ... exhortare eos), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "intensify your battle ... and encourage him" (directing the messenger to encourage Joab).
notes.12:8: The Vulgate renders this condition with a present and future indicative ("if these things are small, I will add"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is usually understood as a past contrafactual ("if that had been too little, I would have added").
notes.12:15: Latin desperatus est literally means "he was despaired of" (that is, his recovery was considered hopeless), corresponding to the Hebrew "he became gravely ill."
notes.12:25: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew name Jedidiah into Latin as Amabilis Domino ("Beloved of the Lord"), preserving the wordplay with the following clause; grammatically, "He" continues the Lord as subject from the end of v. 24.
notes.12:27: Latin capienda est ("is about to be captured") and the preceding imperfect expugnabat ("was storming" in v. 26) portray the capture of the City of Waters as imminent rather than already completed, contrasting with the Hebrew perfect verbs.
notes.12:31: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew idioms as explicit acts of execution ("sawed them," "drove iron-shod carts over them," "cut them apart with knives") and translates the obscure term malben (brick-kiln or brick-mold) literally as in typo laterum ("in the mold of bricks").
notes.13:6: Latin sorbitiunculas ("little broths") reflects the Vulgate's understanding of Tamar's preparation as a liquid invalid's broth (cf. liquefaciens, "making it liquid," in v. 8), where the Hebrew levivot refers to small cakes or dumplings.
notes.13:21: The clause "yet he was unwilling to grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn" is a major Vulgate reading shared with the Septuagint and 4QSam-a but absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.13:27: The concluding sentence, "And Absalom had prepared a feast like the feast of a king," is present in the Vulgate (alongside the Septuagint and 4QSam-a) but absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.13:32: Latin in ore Absalom erat positus literally means "he was placed in the mouth of Absalom," a Semitic idiom indicating that Amnon had been marked for death by Absalom's spoken decree or fixed intention.
notes.13:39: The Vulgate reads the difficult Hebrew clause as David ceasing "to pursue Absalom" (persequi Absalom), whereas the Masoretic Text is commonly understood as David longing to go out to Absalom.
notes.14:11: Vulgate reads plural 'so that the kinsmen of blood may not multiply to take vengeance' (ut non multiplicentur proximi sanguinis ad ulciscendum), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the singular avenger of blood increasing destruction.
notes.14:14: Vulgate distinctively reads 'nor does God wish a soul to perish, but He reconsiders, taking thought' (nec vult Deus perire animam, sed retractat cogitans), where the Hebrew reads 'God does not take away life, but devises plans.'
notes.14:15: Vulgate reads 'in the presence of the people' (praesente populo), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'because the people made me afraid.'
notes.14:17: Vulgate follows the Septuagint in reading 'like a sacrifice' (sicut sacrificium) rather than the Hebrew 'for rest/comfort,' and distinctively renders the next clause 'so that he is moved neither by blessing nor by curse' (ut nec benedictione, nec maledictione moveatur) where the Hebrew reads 'to discern good and evil.'
notes.14:30: The final sentence reporting that Joab's servants came with torn clothes to announce the burning of the field is present in the Vulgate and Septuagint, though absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.15:7: Both the Vulgate (Post quadraginta autem annos) and the Hebrew Masoretic Text read 'forty years,' whereas the Lucianic Greek and the Syriac read 'four years.'
notes.15:18: Vulgate describes the Cherethites and Pelethites as 'legions' (legiones) and adds 'mighty warriors' (pugnatores validi) and 'on foot' (pedites) in describing the six hundred Gittites.
notes.15:20: Vulgate expands the blessing to include 'and the Lord will show mercy and truth toward you, because you have shown grace and faithfulness' (et Dominus faciet tecum misericordiam et veritatem, quia ostendisti gratiam et fidem), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text ends simply with 'steadfast love and faithfulness be with you.'
notes.15:27: Vulgate renders the Hebrew expression as a direct vocative, 'O seer' (O videns), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is often read as a question ('Are you not a seer?') or an imperative ('See!').
notes.15:28: Vulgate reads 'I will hide myself in the plains of the wilderness' (abscondar in campestribus deserti), compared to the Hebrew 'I will linger at the fords/plains of the wilderness.'
notes.16:1: The Vulgate describes the donkeys as "loaded" (onerati erant) rather than "saddled" as in the Masoretic Text, and renders the Hebrew "summer fruit" specifically as "cakes of dried figs" (massis palatharum).
notes.16:10: Latin uses a third-person singular indirect question ("why he has done so," quare sic fecerit), referring primarily to Shimei's cursing, though it may also be understood as referring to the Lord's command.
notes.16:11: Latin filius Jemini ("a son of Jemini") translates the Hebrew gentilic for a Benjaminite literally; Latin de utero meo ("from my womb/belly") is rendered "from my body" in keeping with its sense here for a father's offspring.
notes.16:14: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term as the adjective "weary" (lassus), whereas some interpreters take the Hebrew form (Ayephim) as a place name.
notes.17:3: Distinctively from the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders Ahithophel's comparison as "just as one man usually returns" (quomodo unus homo reverti solet), connecting it to Absalom's search for a single man.
notes.17:11: The Vulgate reads "in their midst" (in medio eorum), reflecting a reading of the Hebrew consonants as qerev ("midst") rather than the Masoretic vocalization qerav ("battle").
notes.17:20: Translating an obscure Hebrew phrase (mikhal ha-mayim, perhaps "the brook of water"), the Vulgate reads "after tasting a little water" (gustata paululum aqua).
notes.17:24: Here and in 17:27, the Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Mahanaim ("two camps") etymologically as a common noun, "into the camp" (in castra).
notes.17:25: The Vulgate identifies Ithra as being "of Jezreel" (de Jezraëli), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "the Israelite" and 1 Chronicles 2:17 reads "the Ishmaelite."
notes.17:29: The Vulgate renders an obscure Hebrew expression for dairy curds or cheese as "fatted calves" (pingues vitulos), alongside similarly distinct Vulgate renderings in 17:28 such as "rugs" (tapetia) and "roasted chickpeas" (frixum cicer).
notes.18:5: The Vulgate reads "Servate mihi puerum Absalom" ("Preserve the boy Absalom for me"), agreeing with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom."
notes.18:14: The Vulgate reads "Non sicut tu vis, sed aggrediar eum coram te" ("Not as you wish, but I will attack him before you"), whereas the Hebrew has "I will not linger like this with you." Later in the verse, the Vulgate uses "palpitaret" ("was still quivering") where the Hebrew has "was still alive."
notes.18:18: The Vulgate renders the name of the monument literally as "Manus Absalom" ("the Hand of Absalom"), reflecting the Hebrew idiom in which "hand" denotes a memorial pillar.
notes.18:21: Throughout verses 21-32, the Vulgate treats "Chusi" (Cushi) as a personal name rather than the gentilic "the Cushite" found in the Hebrew.
notes.18:22: The Vulgate reads "non eris boni nuntii bajulus" ("You will not be a bearer of good news"), whereas the Hebrew reads "you will have no reward for the news."
notes.19:1: Vulgate 19:1 corresponds to 18:33 in the Masoretic Text, shifting all subsequent verse numbers in this chapter ahead by one.
notes.19:4: Vulgate declinavit ... ingredi ("shrank from entering") and versus ("routed") differ from the Masoretic Text, which describes the people stealing secretly into the city like troops ashamed after fleeing battle.
notes.19:17: Latin filii Jemini ("son of Jemini") renders the Hebrew gentilic ben-hayemini ("the Benjaminite") literally as a patronymic.
notes.19:23: Latin in satan uses the untranslated Hebrew loanword meaning "adversary" rather than the proper name of the devil.
notes.19:27: Vulgate contempsit me ("despised me") differs from the Masoretic Text reading "deceived me."
notes.19:33: Vulgate in castris ("in the camp") translates the Hebrew place-name Mahanaim literally.
notes.20:1: Latin vir Belial retains the untranslated Hebrew phrase meaning "a worthless or wicked man," and Jemineus ("Jeminite") reflects the shortened gentilic for a Benjaminite (cf. 19:17).
notes.20:8: The Vulgate describes Joab's sword as deliberately fashioned to come out and strike at a slight movement, whereas the Masoretic Text states that it fell out as he walked.
notes.20:11: The Vulgate has plural soldiers mocking Amasa's corpse as "the one who wanted to be David's companion in place of Joab," whereas the Masoretic Text has a single soldier rallying troops to follow Joab.
notes.20:19: Vulgate "answers truth in Israel" (respondeo veritatem) differs from the Masoretic Text reading "peaceable and faithful in Israel."
notes.20:24: Vulgate super tributa ("over the tribute") translates the Hebrew term for "forced labor," and a commentariis ("recorder") uses a Roman administrative title for a keeper of official records.
notes.21:1: "the oracle of the Lord": the Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom "the face of the Lord" as "oraculum Domini," referring to seeking a divine answer through the sanctuary oracle.
notes.21:6: "crucify" and "once the chosen of the Lord": the Vulgate specifically translates the Hebrew execution verb as crucifixion here ("crucifigamus"), in v. 9 ("crucifixerunt"), and in v. 13 ("affixi fuerant," "had been affixed"), and adds "once" ("quondam") to note Saul's former status as the Lord's chosen.
notes.21:14: "on the side": the Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Zela (literally "side" or "rib") as a common noun phrase ("in latere").
notes.21:16: "Arapha" and "the iron of whose spear weighed three hundred ounces": the Vulgate fuses the Hebrew definite article with "raphah" into the proper name Arapha (vv. 16, 18, 20, 22; paired with "of the race of the giants" in v. 18), and specifies three hundred ounces of iron rather than three hundred shekels of bronze.
notes.21:19: "Adeodatus the son of Saltus, an embroiderer": the Vulgate translates the Hebrew name Elhanan as the Latin name Adeodatus ("Given by God"), Jaare as Saltus ("Forest"), and oregim as the trade "embroiderer" ("polymitarius"), while naming his opponent simply "Goliath the Gittite" as in the Masoretic Text (cf. 1 Chronicles 20:5).
notes.22:3: The Vulgate translates Hebrew "rock" (tsur) as fortis ("strong") here and in vv. 32 and 47, and renders the Hebrew "stronghold/high refuge" literally with the agent noun elevator ("the One who lifts me up").
notes.22:12: The Vulgate reads cribrans aquas ("sifting waters"), a distinctive rendering of the difficult Hebrew phrase usually understood as "a gathering of waters."
notes.22:19: The Vulgate has the singular verb praevenit ("he confronted me"), referring back to the singular "most powerful enemy" of v. 18 (though some commentators refer it to the Lord coming beforehand to meet David), whereas the Hebrew has the plural "they confronted me."
notes.22:30: The Vulgate reads curram accinctus ("I will run girded"), differing from the Hebrew "I can run against a troop."
notes.22:45: The Vulgate reads resistent mihi ("will resist me"), whereas the Hebrew verb expresses cringing or feigned submission.
notes.23:1: The Vulgate reads cui constitutum est de christo Dei Jacob ("to whom it was appointed concerning the anointed of the God of Jacob"), where the Hebrew reads "the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob."
notes.23:5: The Vulgate reads a negative statement ("Nor is my house so great before God that He should enter into an eternal covenant with me"), where the Masoretic Text has a rhetorical question ("Is not my house so with God? For He has made with me an everlasting covenant").
notes.23:8: Rather than transliterating the Hebrew proper names (Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite and Adino the Eznite), the Vulgate translates them etymologically as "the one sitting in the chair, the wisest chief" and "like the most tender little worm of wood."
notes.23:9: The Vulgate translates Hebrew ben-dodo literally as "the son of his uncle" (filius patrui ejus) rather than treating Dodo as a personal name (so also in 23:24).
notes.23:23: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for David's bodyguard (mishma'at, derived from the root "to hear") as auricularium, a secreto, denoting a confidential counselor in charge of secret affairs.
notes.24:1: The Vulgate uses the accusative participle dicentem agreeing with David ("stirred up David ... to say"), making David rather than the Lord the immediate speaker of the command to number Israel and Judah.
notes.24:4: After referring to plural "commanders of the army" (principum exercitus) in the first clause, the Clementine Vulgate reads singular princeps militum ("the commander of the soldiers") in the second clause.
notes.24:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew place names Tahtim-hodshi and Dan-jaan descriptively as "the lower land of Hodshi" (terram inferiorem Hodsi) and "the woodlands of Dan" (Dan silvestria).
notes.24:23: The Vulgate reads nominative Areuna rex regi ("Araunah the king gave ... to the king"), matching the Hebrew consonantal text where "the king" stands in apposition to Araunah rather than as a vocative, and reads "accept your vow" (suscipiat votum tuum) where the Hebrew has "accept you."
